data.title: Furuncle and carbuncle — viva
data.summary: Bacterial infections · 9 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Furuncle and carbuncle** (Bacterial infections)_

**Q1. Define furuncle and carbuncle.**
- Furuncle (boil): acute deep necrotising infection of a hair follicle by S. aureus with perifollicular abscess, central necrotic core
- Carbuncle: confluent furuncles involving several adjacent follicles with multiple draining points (sieve-like), deeper, on nape/back/thighs, with fever and malaise

**Q2. Risk factors?**
- Nasal/perineal carriage of S. aureus, diabetes, obesity, poor hygiene, friction and sweating, immunodeficiency (HIV, steroids), atopic dermatitis, iron deficiency, PVL-producing community MRSA, chronic granulomatous disease/hyper-IgE (recurrent)

**Q3. Sites of predilection?**
- Hair-bearing areas exposed to friction: neck, face, axillae, buttocks, thighs; not on palms/soles (no follicles)

**Q4. Why is a furuncle on the central face dangerous?**
- Danger triangle — spread via angular and ophthalmic veins to cavernous sinus (cavernous sinus thrombosis); avoid squeezing

**Q5. Investigations in recurrent furunculosis?**
- Pus culture/sensitivity (MRSA, PVL), nasal/perineal/axillary swabs of patient and family, blood sugar, CBC, HIV, immunoglobulins/neutrophil function if childhood onset

**Q6. Treatment?**
- Warm compresses; incision and drainage when fluctuant (main treatment for abscess)
- Antibiotics if large, multiple, cellulitis, fever, immunocompromised, central face: cloxacillin, cephalexin, amoxicillin–clavulanate; MRSA: co-trimoxazole, doxycycline, clindamycin, linezolid

**Q7. Management of recurrent furunculosis (decolonisation)?**
- Nasal mupirocin twice daily × 5 days (monthly for some months), chlorhexidine 4% body washes, bleach baths, wash linen/towels hot, treat family carriers
- Long-term low-dose clindamycin 150 mg/day × 3 months, or rifampicin 600 mg/day × 10 days with another antistaphylococcal agent, or vitamin C (neutrophil function)

**Q8. What is bacterial interference therapy?**
- Deliberate colonisation of nares with a non-virulent S. aureus strain (502A) to prevent recolonisation by virulent strains — historical

**Q9. What is botryomycosis?**
- Chronic suppurative granulomatous bacterial infection (usually S. aureus) forming grains — mimics mycetoma/actinomycosis

## Quick spotter facts
- Painful red nodule with central pus point on the buttock — furuncle

_Sources: DYP Survival Guide for PG Dermatology Exam (Bacterial infections — furuncle, carbuncle, recurrent furunculosis); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e ch.15. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
